claims.text: Rapid solidification inherent to additive manufacturing promotes localized elemental segregation in the alloy.
The as-manufactured alloy has a non-uniform distribution of Cr and Al.
Elemental heterogeneity drives formation of a dual-layer oxide scale during elevated-temperature exposure.
Oxidizing exposure produces a thin, adherent, Al/Cr-rich outer oxide layer that provides moderate protection.
The protective Al/Cr-rich layer is less stable under reducing conditions.
Reduced stability of the oxide layer permits faster internal diffusion and phase-boundary oxidation, degrading surface integrity.
The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy initially has an fcc matrix.
The initial alloy exhibits microsegregation caused by rapid solidification.
The oxide scale contains spatially distinct Al/Cr-rich outer regions and Ti-enriched or otherwise less-protective inner regions.
In oxidizing atmospheres, Al and Cr diffuse preferentially to form a partially protective oxide scale.
Under reducing conditions, instability of Al- and Cr-containing oxides, potentially influenced by Ti, causes scale disruption and grain-boundary degradation.
Oxidizing exposure will produce a relatively uniform and adherent scale that slows subsequent oxidation.
Reducing exposure will produce more scale spallation or discontinuities than oxidizing exposure.
Scale discontinuities under reducing exposure will act as initiation sites for degradation.
The fcc matrix will remain largely intact during the proposed exposures.
The proposed behavior applies approximately from 700 to 900 °C, provided exposure occurs before a bulk phase transformation compromises the fcc matrix.
Post-processing homogenization can modify the degree of microsegregation while enabling comparison under otherwise identical exposures.
Changing microsegregation should alter oxide-scale formation and degradation rates differently in oxidizing and reducing atmospheres.
